title: Root: *finis* (boundary, end) — the limit shared, the limit unset, the limit reached
core: Every word here is built on Latin *finis*, a boundary line — the edge where one thing stops and the next begins. The family splits by what each word does with that edge: one word puts two things on either side of the same border, one refuses to draw the border at all, and one works a thing up to its finished edge. Knowing the root gets you into the neighbourhood but not to the door, because the surface meanings — kinship, vagueness, polishing — look unrelated until you see the line underneath.

words.nuance: **Affinity** is *ad-finis*: sharing a border, next door. It is the only word here describing a relation **between two things**, and it insists the connection was already there — not developed, not earned. Preference you formed is taste; **affinity** is fit you discovered.

**Indefinite** is the only negative member: the boundary was never drawn. Note it says nothing about length — an **indefinite** suspension may end Tuesday. What it reports is the *speaker's* refusal to specify, which is why it turns cold in official prose ("held indefinitely") in a way the others never do.

**Refine** treats the edge as a destination — bring it to *fine*, the finished state. The only verb, and the only word implying labour and improvement: something already sound gets impurity stripped and edges smoothed. Nothing is added, nothing rebuilt; you **refine** a decent model, you overhaul a broken one.

exam_note: The classic traps are near-homophone drift: **indefinite** misread as *infinite* (endless) when it means merely unspecified, and **affinity** misread as chosen fondness when the point is inherent kinship.
